questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with a compromised immune system about safe food handling during hospitalization, after the client's family brought in a fruit platter and some homemade deli sandwiches from a local shop. Which recommendation is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No special food-related precautions at all being needed for this particular client despite their compromised immune status right now at this time","B":"Freely sharing food and eating utensils with other clients on the same unit, including the items the family just brought in earlier today","C":"Eating raw or undercooked meat and eggs being considered perfectly safe for this particular population of immunocompromised clients right now","D":"Avoiding raw or undercooked meats, unpasteurized dairy, and unwashed produce, and being cautious about deli meats and other higher-risk foods like those the family brought in"}}
questions.rationale: Immunocompromised clients are at increased risk for foodborne illness, so guidance typically includes avoiding raw or undercooked meats/eggs, unpasteurized dairy products, and unwashed produce, along with other food safety precautions to reduce infection risk.
questions.source_name: CDC — Food Safety for People with Weakened Immune Systems
questions.source_detail: Food Safety Precautions for Immunocompromised Individuals

questions.stem: A nurse is communicating with a client who has a significant hearing impairment. Which technique is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Facing the client directly, speaking clearly at a normal pace, and ensuring adequate lighting for lip-reading if needed","B":"Shouting loudly at the client from across the room to ensure the message is heard","C":"Deliberately covering the mouth with a hand or mask while speaking to the client","D":"Avoiding any visual cues or written communication when interacting with the client"}}
questions.rationale: Effective communication with a hearing-impaired client includes facing the client directly (to support lip-reading if used), speaking clearly at a normal pace and volume (not necessarily shouting, which can distort sounds), ensuring good lighting, and using written communication or interpreters as needed.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Communication with Sensory-Impaired Clients

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client with significant visual impairment. Which communication approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Rearranging the client's room and belongings frequently without informing them first","B":"Assuming the client is unable to participate meaningfully in their own care decisions","C":"Avoiding any verbal description of the surrounding environment during care","D":"Announcing one's presence upon entering the room, orienting the client to the environment, and using clear verbal descriptions"}}
questions.rationale: Effective communication with a visually impaired client includes announcing one's presence when entering the room, orienting the client to their environment (especially if items are moved), and using clear, descriptive verbal communication, since visual cues are not available to convey this information.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Communication with Sensory-Impaired Clients

questions.stem: After a lumbar puncture, a client asks the nurse whether they can sit up now to eat the lunch tray that just arrived. The nurse typically positions the client, and should advise the client to remain, in which position?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"In a prone position with the head of the bed elevated for the client's own comfort while eating their lunch tray","B":"Standing upright and ambulating in the hallway immediately after the procedure to encourage better circulation","C":"Sitting fully upright in a chair immediately following the procedure so the client can eat comfortably right away","D":"Lying flat, per provider orders/protocol, to help reduce the risk of a post-procedure headache, meaning the lunch tray should wait"}}
questions.rationale: After a lumbar puncture, clients are often positioned lying flat for a period per provider orders or facility protocol, which may help reduce the risk of a post-lumbar puncture headache (caused by cerebrospinal fluid leakage), along with adequate hydration.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Post-Lumbar Puncture Care
questions.source_detail: Positioning to Reduce Post-Procedure Headache Risk

questions.stem: A nurse is providing health promotion teaching to an older adult client about recommended adult immunizations. Which vaccines are commonly recommended for this age group, per CDC guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No vaccines at all are recommended for adults once they reach age 65","B":"Shingles (herpes zoster) and pneumococcal vaccines, among others, based on age and risk factors","C":"Only the MMR vaccine, with no other vaccine recommended for this age group","D":"Only the varicella vaccine, with no other vaccine recommended for this age group"}}
questions.rationale: CDC adult immunization schedules recommend several vaccines for older adults based on age and risk factors, commonly including the shingles (herpes zoster) vaccine and pneumococcal vaccines, in addition to routine vaccines like annual influenza and updated COVID-19 vaccines.
questions.source_name: CDC — Recommended Adult Immunization Schedule
questions.source_detail: Age-Based Vaccine Recommendations for Older Adults

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a pregnant client with an uncomplicated pregnancy about exercise. Which guidance is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular moderate-intensity exercise is generally safe and recommended for most pregnant individuals without contraindications, per ACOG guidance","B":"Only strict bed rest is recommended for the client throughout the entire pregnancy","C":"Exercise intensity should always be increased throughout pregnancy regardless of symptoms","D":"All physical exercise should be avoided completely throughout the entire pregnancy"}}
questions.rationale: ACOG guidance generally recommends regular moderate-intensity physical activity for most pregnant individuals without medical or obstetric contraindications, as it offers benefits for both maternal and fetal health, with specific activity modifications as pregnancy progresses.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy

questions.stem: A nurse is helping a client develop strategies to improve medication adherence for a chronic condition. Which strategy is likely to be most helpful?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Providing no specific strategies, since adherence is considered solely the client's responsibility","B":"Avoiding any discussion of the client's specific barriers to taking the medication","C":"Simplifying the medication regimen when possible, using pill organizers, and linking doses to daily routines","D":"Increasing the overall complexity of the medication regimen to improve tracking"}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based strategies to improve medication adherence include simplifying the regimen when possible (e.g., reducing dosing frequency), using tools like pill organizers or reminder apps, and linking medication times to established daily routines, along with addressing individual barriers the client identifies.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Medication Adherence Improvement Strategies

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client whose family reports a significant, unexplained weight loss over the past several months, along with the client insisting they are "still too heavy" despite appearing visibly underweight. Which additional finding would be most consistent with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excessive exercise occurring in isolation, with no other accompanying symptom present alongside the weight loss described","B":"Significantly restricted food intake, an intense fear of gaining weight, and the distorted body image already being described by the family","C":"Overeating episodes accompanied by a distinct sense of loss of control, a pattern not consistent with the weight loss described here","D":"A complete absence of any concern about the client's own body weight or shape, contrary to what the family has actually described"}}
questions.rationale: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by significantly restricted food intake leading to a low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight, and a distorted perception of one's own body weight or shape, distinct from binge eating disorder, which involves episodes of overeating with a sense of loss of control.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Anorexia Nervosa
questions.source_detail: Core Diagnostic Features of Anorexia Nervosa

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a child with autism spectrum disorder who becomes visibly distressed when a routine blood draw is introduced without warning partway through the shift. Which communication approach should the nurse have used, and should continue to use going forward?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Using clear, concrete language, maintaining consistent routines, and allowing extra time for processing before introducing something new","B":"Using frequent abstract or figurative language when communicating with the child about upcoming procedures","C":"Avoiding any structure or predictability in interactions with the child throughout the shift","D":"Making frequent, unexpected changes to the child's established care routine, similar to what just happened with the blood draw"}}
questions.rationale: Effective communication with a child with autism spectrum disorder generally includes using clear, concrete (rather than abstract or figurative) language, maintaining consistent routines and predictability, and allowing extra time for the child to process information and respond, since these approaches support understanding and reduce anxiety.
questions.source_name: Autism Speaks / AAP — Communication Strategies for Autism Spectrum Disorder

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a school-age child for possible ADHD after the teacher reported concerns, but the parents mention the behaviors only seem to happen at school and not at home. Which finding would actually be most consistent with this diagnosis, given the DSM criteria requiring symptoms across multiple settings?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A single, isolated incident of inattention observed during just one classroom visit made by the teacher earlier this term","B":"Persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity inconsistent with developmental level, impairing functioning across more than one setting","C":"Symptoms present in only the school setting for a period of less than one week, as the parents are currently describing","D":"Excellent, sustained attention span with no behavioral concerns of any kind reported in either the school or home setting"}}
questions.rationale: ADHD is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is inconsistent with the child's developmental level, present in multiple settings (such as home and school), and causes functional impairment — not a single isolated incident or brief, situation-specific behavior.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — ADHD Diagnostic Guidelines

questions.stem: A client is given naloxone in the emergency department for an opioid overdose involving a long-acting opioid, and initially improves enough to speak and open their eyes. The nurse should continue close monitoring for an extended period because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Naloxone's duration is often shorter than many opioids, especially long-acting ones, so respiratory depression can recur as it wears off","B":"No further monitoring being needed once the initial naloxone dose has produced this kind of improvement in the client","C":"Naloxone permanently reversing every opioid effect for the rest of the client's system, eliminating any further overdose risk","D":"The client can be safely discharged immediately after receiving just this one naloxone dose in the emergency department"}}
questions.rationale: Naloxone's duration of action (roughly 30-120 minutes) is often shorter than that of the opioid causing the overdose, particularly with long-acting or high-potency opioids. This creates a risk of renarcotization (recurrence of respiratory depression) as the naloxone wears off, requiring continued close monitoring and possible repeat dosing.
questions.source_name: Naloxone Dosing Strategies — Poison Control Clinical Guidance

questions.stem: A client is prescribed buprenorphine as part of medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder, and a family member asks whether this just replaces one addiction with another, similar to using heroin. The nurse understands this medication:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A full opioid agonist carrying just the same overdose risk as an illicit opioid like heroin","B":"A medication that should rarely if ever be combined with any counseling or behavioral treatment approach","C":"Is a partial opioid agonist that reduces cravings and withdrawal while carrying a lower overdose risk than full agonists like heroin","D":"A medication with fairly little established role in the treatment of opioid use disorder, despite being prescribed for exactly that purpose here"}}
questions.rationale: Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist used in medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder. It helps reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms, and due to its "ceiling effect" on respiratory depression, it carries a lower overdose risk compared to full opioid agonists, though it is not risk-free, especially combined with other CNS depressants.
questions.source_name: SAMHSA — Medication-Assisted Treatment for Opioid Use Disorder
questions.source_detail: Buprenorphine as a Partial Agonist Treatment

questions.stem: A client receiving methadone maintenance therapy is also newly prescribed an antibiotic known to prolong the QT interval, and the nurse notices this combination in the medication list. The nurse should recognize methadone itself already carries which cardiac risk that is now compounded by the new antibiotic?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excessive salivation and sweating, changes unrelated to the QT-prolonging risk this particular medication combination actually poses here","B":"A drop in resting heart rate, an effect not primarily linked to either methadone or the newly added antibiotic in this regimen","C":"An improvement in overall cardiac conduction, with fairly little associated cardiac risk from either medication being given to this client","D":"QT interval prolongation, which can increase the risk of a life-threatening arrhythmia, a particular concern now that a second QT-prolonging medication has been added"}}
questions.rationale: Methadone is associated with dose-dependent QT interval prolongation, which can increase the risk of Torsades de Pointes, a life-threatening arrhythmia. Baseline and periodic ECG monitoring is recommended, particularly at higher doses or with other risk factors for QT prolongation.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Methadone

questions.stem: A client taking disulfiram for alcohol use disorder mentions they plan to use a particular brand of mouthwash that a friend recommended and also enjoys cooking with wine-based sauces. The nurse should teach the client to strictly avoid:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"All forms of alcohol, including hidden sources like some mouthwashes and cooking wine, due to a severe reaction with this medication","B":"Caffeine intake specifically, with fairly little particular concern regarding the alcohol sources the client just mentioned","C":"Any form of physical activity, since exercise is thought by some to trigger a severe reaction with this particular medication","D":"Spicy foods, which carry little particular concern for someone taking this medication"}}
questions.rationale: Disulfiram causes a severe, unpleasant reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, potentially dangerous cardiovascular effects) when combined with even small amounts of alcohol, including hidden sources such as certain mouthwashes, cooking wine, or some medications, requiring careful client education about all potential alcohol sources.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Disulfiram

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a pregnant client in her first trimester who takes lithium for bipolar disorder and is considering stopping the medication entirely on her own out of fear for the baby. The nurse should be aware that lithium use during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, carries an increased risk of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only potential maternal risks, since this medication is treated as carrying no known fetal implications worth discussing further","B":"An improvement in fetal cardiac development specifically associated with maternal lithium use during this particular trimester","C":"No fetal risk whatsoever being associated with maternal lithium use during pregnancy, meaning the client's fear would be unfounded","D":"Ebstein's anomaly, a rare cardiac malformation, among other risks, warranting a careful risk-benefit talk with the provider rather than stopping alone"}}
questions.rationale: Lithium use during pregnancy, particularly during the first trimester, has been associated with an increased risk of Ebstein's anomaly, a rare congenital heart defect, among other potential risks. Treatment decisions require careful individualized risk-benefit discussion between the client and provider.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Lithium

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a client of childbearing age who is newly prescribed valproate for seizure control and mentions she is not currently using any form of contraception. The nurse should emphasize that this medication carries a boxed warning for:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Neural tube defects and decreased IQ in offspring if taken during pregnancy, warranting effective contraception and preconception counseling","B":"No significant pregnancy-related risks associated with taking this medication, so the client's lack of contraception is not a particular concern","C":"Only mild, clinically inconsequential effects on the fetus if the medication happens to be taken throughout an entire pregnancy","D":"An improvement in fetal neurodevelopment specifically associated with maternal use of this medication during pregnancy"}}
questions.rationale: FDA labeling includes a boxed warning that valproate can cause fetal harm, including neural tube defects and decreased IQ scores, when taken during pregnancy. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception, and preconception counseling is essential given the significant teratogenic risk.
questions.source_name: FDA — Boxed Warning for Valproate Products
questions.source_detail: Neural Tube Defect and Cognitive Risk in Pregnancy

questions.stem: A client taking an ACE inhibitor for hypertension discovers she is 6 weeks pregnant and asks whether she should just wait until the second trimester to worry about switching medications. The nurse should recognize that ACE inhibitors are:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A concern limited only to the first trimester, meaning the client's plan to wait would actually be appropriate for the rest of pregnancy","B":"Generally contraindicated during pregnancy, particularly in the second and third trimesters, due to risk of fetal renal damage","C":"Safe to continue taking throughout the entirety of pregnancy with no associated maternal or fetal concern at any point","D":"The preferred first-line antihypertensive medication choice during pregnancy, offering the best fetal safety profile of any option"}}
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors are generally contraindicated during pregnancy, particularly in the second and third trimesters, due to the risk of fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios, and other serious complications. The client should be promptly referred to her provider to discuss alternative antihypertensive options.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — ACE Inhibitors
questions.source_detail: Contraindication in Pregnancy: Fetal Renal Risk

questions.stem: A laboring client receives epidural anesthesia, and shortly afterward the fetal monitor shows a subtle deceleration pattern. The nurse should first consider monitoring closely for which common maternal adverse effect that could explain this fetal change?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hyperglycemia, a metabolic effect not typically associated with epidural anesthesia or the fetal monitor change being described here","B":"Hypertension, essentially the opposite of the typical hemodynamic effect of epidural anesthesia and not the likely explanation in this particular case","C":"Hypotension, due to sympathetic blockade, requiring frequent blood pressure monitoring, since maternal hypotension can explain fetal deceleration patterns like this one","D":"Bradypnea alone, with fairly little associated effect on the client's blood pressure or the fetal monitor tracing shown here"}}
questions.rationale: Epidural anesthesia causes sympathetic nervous system blockade, which can lead to maternal hypotension. Frequent blood pressure monitoring, adequate IV hydration, and positioning (avoiding supine position) are standard nursing interventions to reduce this risk and its impact on fetal perfusion.
questions.source_name: ACOG / ASA — Obstetric Anesthesia Practice Guidelines

questions.stem: A client receiving a prolonged, high-dose sodium nitroprusside infusion for hypertensive emergency should be monitored for signs of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An improvement in the client's overall thyroid gland function during the infusion","B":"Cyanide toxicity, a rare but serious risk with prolonged or high-dose use","C":"Hypoglycemia, a metabolic effect not typically associated with this medication","D":"No significant risks are associated with this medication at any dose or duration"}}
questions.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside is metabolized to cyanide, and prolonged infusion or high doses (particularly with renal or hepatic impairment) carry a risk of cyanide toxicity, presenting with symptoms such as altered mental status, metabolic acidosis, and hemodynamic instability, requiring close monitoring.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Sodium Nitroprusside

questions.stem: A client taking isotretinoin for severe acne mentions to the nurse feeling "more down than usual" over the past couple of weeks but assumes it's unrelated to the medication. In addition to teratogenicity, the nurse should be aware that isotretinoin carries warnings related to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Possible mood changes, including depression, meaning the client's symptoms should be taken seriously and reported to the provider rather than assumed unrelated","B":"A guaranteed improvement in mood reported by every client taking this medication, contrary to what this client is actually describing","C":"No psychiatric risk of any kind associated with this medication, contrary to what this client is currently experiencing","D":"Risk limited only to physical side effects, with no psychiatric component requiring any monitoring at all, contrary to what this client is describing"}}
questions.rationale: In addition to its well-known teratogenic risk, isotretinoin labeling includes precautions regarding possible mood changes, including depression, and clients (and their families) should be counseled to monitor for and promptly report any new or worsening mood or behavioral changes during treatment.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Isotretinoin
